channel.title: Contact Sheet Demo
channel.description: A WordPress theme for photographers and image lovers

item.title: The Flower That Outlived the Republic
item.content:encoded: The country that built it no longer exists, but the monument still opens its concrete petals to the weather. Up close the utopian smoothness has gone to lichen and rust-stain; from the road it still stops you cold — a flower the size of a house, blooming for a future that changed its mind.

item.title: Saturday at the Palace of Culture
item.content:encoded: The chandeliers are the originals and so, it seems, are some of the coats. A wedding on the mezzanine, a chess club in the side room, kids skidding across the terrazzo — the great concrete palace was built for exactly this and simply never stopped. Utopia, it turns out, keeps decent opening hours.

item.title: The People's Circus Still Turns
item.content:encoded: A perfect concrete drum on the edge of town, its ribbed roof built to look like a spinning top mid-spin. Inside, the ring still fills on weekends; outside, the great cantilevered canopy throws the same shadow it has thrown for fifty years. Not everything Soviet was grey — some of it was a literal big top, poured in cement.

item.title: Stacked City: The Highways Megastructure
item.content:encoded: They stacked the offices like a game of Jenga left mid-move — horizontal concrete bars flung across a ravine, holding air where a building should be solid. It was built for a ministry of roads; it now houses a bank, and the forest has climbed halfway up its legs. Fifty years on it still looks like it was finished tomorrow.

item.title: The White Tower Still Thinks
item.content:encoded: A research institute shaped like a proof: a slim white tower ringed by cantilevered floors, built to say that the future would be clean, rational and Soviet. The equipment inside has changed a dozen times; the tower hasn't. It still hums quietly on its hill, thinking whatever tall white towers think.

item.title: Taking the Waters, Still
item.content:encoded: The brochures promised sunshine, mineral baths and a better socialist body, and against all odds the place still delivers. Guests in robes drift along the curved balconies; the sea glitters below exactly as advertised. A working monument to the idea that rest, too, could be engineered — and rather beautifully.

item.title: The Saucer on the Hill
item.content:encoded: You climb for an hour and it never quite looks real: a concrete flying saucer beached on a mountaintop, ringed by fog, its great round hall open to the sky where the roof has failed. Inside, mosaic still clings to the ceiling in fields of red and gold. The most ambitious building nobody uses — and the most unforgettable.

item.title: Ghost Auditorium
item.content:encoded: Fifteen hundred seats face a stage no one will light again. Dust hangs in the one blade of daylight that finds the hall; the concrete acoustic canopy still curves overhead, waiting for a note. It is the silence that gets you — a room designed to be full, holding perfectly still.

The Radar at the Edge of the Zone
item.content:encoded: It is less a building than a horizon: a wall of steel lattice half a kilometre long and thirty storeys high, built to hear the far side of the world. It heard nothing worth keeping and was switched off, but it still stands in the forest like a rusting harp, too vast and too strange to ever quite abandon.

item.title: Microrayon Mornings
item.content:encoded: Twelve identical towers around a shared yard, and every window a small argument with sameness: a glassed-in balcony here, a bright new paint job there, laundry, a satellite dish angled at a different sky. The planners drew a machine for living; the residents have spent fifty years turning it, patiently, back into a neighbourhood.

item.title: A Thousand Balconies, All Different Now
item.content:encoded: From across the street it is one enormous grid; step closer and it dissolves into a thousand private decisions. Every loggia glazed, boarded, painted or planted to its owner's taste, until the block becomes a mosaic of small freedoms laid over the architect's rigid staves.

item.title: Monuments to Gagarin's Sky
item.content:encoded: They built the future in titanium and concrete and pointed all of it upward — a rocket frozen mid-launch on a soaring metal arc, a cosmonaut striding into a stylized wind. Grandiose, sincere, and still strangely moving: monuments to the brief moment when the sky belonged to everyone.

item.title: Concrete Stars: A Spomenik Survey
item.content:encoded: They were built to be seen from a distance and understood by everyone — abstract, wordless, enormous. Ten monuments scattered across hills and battlefields, each a different idea of how concrete might hold grief and hope at once. Photographed the same way every time, they become a constellation: stars poured in cement, still burning on their empty ridges.

item.title: Tskaltubo, Reclaimed by Ferns
item.content:encoded: The spa town emptied when the union did, and the forest moved in to take the waters instead. Ferns unfurl on the bathhouse floors, daylight pours through a collapsed dome onto a grand empty staircase, and the whole complex holds its breath — too beautiful to demolish, too broken to reopen. Worth every hour of the drive.

item.title: Tarilka: The Flying Saucer of Kyiv
item.content:encoded: Locals just call it the saucer. A perfect ribbed concrete disc balanced on a squat cylinder, built for an institute of scientific information and looking every inch ready for takeoff. Half its offices still work; the other half dream. Either way it remains the most optimistic roofline in the city.

item.title: About the theme
item.content:encoded:
This is a demo site built to showcase Contact Sheet, a free WordPress theme for photographers and every other kind of image lover. The theme was created by Matias Benedetto and is available for anyone to install from the WordPress.org theme directory.

Contact Sheet keeps the interface out of the way and lets your pictures carry the page: on the home and archive views your posts are laid out as a film-inspired contact strip, and each post shows its photographs full width, one after another.

How to use it

  • Install the theme from Appearance → Themes → Add New in your WordPress dashboard (search for “Contact Sheet”), or download it from the theme directory.
  • Create a post for each set of photos. Add your pictures as Image blocks in the post body — they appear stacked below your text.
  • The first image of every post becomes its thumbnail in the contact-sheet grid on the home page and archives.
  • Personalise the site from the Editor: set a site icon and logo, a tagline, colours and fonts, and the navigation menu.

About the images

Every photograph on this demo — the Soviet-era monuments and buildings, and even the portrait used as the site icon — was generated with AI (Google Imagen) from written prompts. None of them are real photographs; they exist purely to demonstrate how the theme presents image-heavy content.

Free and open source

Contact Sheet is free software, released under the GNU General Public License (GPL). You can use it at no cost on as many sites as you like, study how it works, modify it to fit your needs, and share your own derived versions under the same licence. Build on it freely.
